new_statements.quote: Primary stress (ˊ) is the higher of the two in intensity and always occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. [ˈda.gan] /dagan/ 'to sell' [ka.ˈo.man] /kaoman/ 'precinct' [...] Perturbation of stress occurs upon affixation giving evidence that stress is a feature of the rhythm segment itself, and is not a phonetic characteristic of a particular word root. Upon affixation, stress always moves to the nucleus of the penultimate syllable of the rhythm segment: [ˈla.bas] /labas/ 'to cut underbrush' [li.ˈa.bas] /liabas/ 'cut the underbrush' [li.a.ˈba.san] /liabasan/ 'cleared of underbrush' [li.a.ba.ˈsan.nu] /liabasannu/ 'you clear it of underbrush'
new_statements.citation: Walton, Charles. 1979. Pangutaran (Sama) phonology. Studies in Philippine Linguistics 3(2): 189-217. Manila: Linguistic Society of the Philippines & Summer Institute of Linguistics.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (29-page scan, no text layer; scanned in the. beside it) and rendered scan page 4 (printed p. 191) and scan page 5 (p. 192) to PNG and read the page images. The quoted passage is on p. 191, section 2.1 'Primary Stress', exactly as reported: 'Primary stress (´) is the higher of the two in intensity and always occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word. [´da.gan] /dagan/ 'to sell' [ka.´o.man] /kaoman/ 'precinct'... Perturbation of stress occurs upon affixation giving evidence that stress is a feature of the rhythm segment itself, and is not a phonetic characteristic of a particular word root. Upon affixation, stress always moves to the nucleus of the penultimate syllable of the rhy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word ('rhythm segment'), counted after all affixation and encliticisation, so it shifts rightward with every suffix or enclitic (labas > liabas > liabasan > liabasannu). Stress is realised as a slight pitch rise, loudness and length on the nucleus (length is absent when the penult vowel is schwa). Every word has at least two syllables; surface monosyllables with long vowels ([ˈso:] 'snake', [ˈbu:d] 'mountain') are analysed as two identical vowel syllables with stress on the first, which keeps the penult rule exceptionless.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 192, sec. 2.2: 'Secondary stress is a feature of rhythm segments consisting of more than three syllables. It is characterized by less intensity than primary stress and occurs on the second syllable preceding the penultimate syllable in words having more than three syllables' ([ˌpi.bal.ˈli.han] /piballihan/ 'to sell', [ta.ˌpi.bal.ˈli.han] 'can be sold', [ˌhi.lu.ˈha.laŋ] 'to make noise'); 'In words having more than five syllables an additional secondary stress occurs on the fourth syllable preceding the penultimate syllable of the word' ([ˌmag.ka.ˌsa.u.ˈda.gal] /magkasaudagal/ 'to become rich'). I.e. right-aligned alternating (trochaic) rhythm leftward from the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions: 'stress only occurs on the penultimate syllable in nonsuspect data' (p. 194) and 'the penultimate syllable always carries stress' (p. 195); the penult analysis is used as the criterion for interpreting vocoid sequences and long vowels. Phonetic caveats: schwa penult is not lengthened ([ˈkəlloq] 'to fetch'); phrase stress, a feature of the pause segment (clause), 'often obscures the primary stress of the rhythm segment since it usually does not occur on the penultimate syllable of a word', e.g. when it falls on the final syllable of the pause group with high intonation (p. 191); primary stress is best observed on non-final words of the phrase. Footnote 4 (p. 217): the only syllable-final glottal stop before a consonant, /taqban/, is a Tausug loan (a segmental, not stress, note).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'rhythm segment' = phonological word, which 'generally... is one grammatical word but in many instances it is [a] grammatical phrase' (p. 189); stress is assigned to the affixed/encliticised word (suffix -an and enclitic -nu count). Word-level stress is distinguished from phrase stress of the pause segment (clause) and from five intonation contours (sec. 5). Data are from monolingual elicitation and texts, not citation forms only.
new_statements.identity_note: Walton 1979 describes Pangutaran (Sama) = Pangutaran Sama [slm] / pang1291 (Glottolog attaches the paper to this languoid). Footnote 2 (p. 217): the research was done Oct 1975-Apr 1976 in Kompang on Cagayan de Sulu (Mapun island), one of three Pangutaran-speaking communities there (~1,000 speakers), i.e. a migrant colony rather than Pangutaran Island itself (~10,000 speakers); the author treats it as the same language and gives no dialect label. Not to be confused with Mapun/Cagayan de Sulu Sama [sjm, mapu1244], the majority language of that island.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'Rhythm Segment' (= phonological word): primary stress always on the penultimate syllable of the word/rhythm segment and moves rightward under affixation and encliticisation; secondary stress on the 2nd syllable before the penult in words of >3 syllables and again 4 syllables before the penult in words of >5 syllables; a separate phrase stress belongs to the pause segment and can obscure word stress on the final word.
